Cyrano de Bergerac is most famously an 1897 verse play by Edmond Rostand, though it is based on a real 17th-century French polymath.

The Famous Play

The drama tells the story of Cyrano, a brilliant poet and expert swordsman with an enormous nose that makes him believe he is too ugly to be loved. He secretly adores his cousin Roxane, but instead of wooing her himself, he uses his poetic genius to write letters for the handsome but dim-witted Christian. This creates a tragic love triangle where Roxane falls in love with Christian's face but Cyrano's soul. It popularized the concept of "panache"—a flamboyant style and courageous spirit maintained even in the face of defeat.

The Real Person

Savinien de Cyrano de Bergerac (1619–1655) was an actual French soldier, duelist, and pioneering writer. While he did have a large nose and a reputation for bravado, he was also a radical philosopher and an early pioneer of science fiction. His works, such as The Other World: Comical History of the States and Empires of the Moon, imagined space travel and advanced civilizations long before the genre was established.
